title: Michael Stoner, German long hunter
summary: Born Michael Holsteiner near Philadelphia in 1748, Stoner rode with Daniel Boone in 1774 to warn surveyors across Kentucky ahead of Dunmore’s War.
bodyMarkdown:
[Michael Stoner](/people/#michael-stoner) was born Michael Holsteiner, to German parents, near Philadelphia in 1748. He spoke English all his life with a thick German accent. At about sixteen he headed for the New River country of Virginia, and by 1767 he was at Fort Pitt.

That year he joined Samuel Harrod, older brother of Harrodsburg's founder, on a long hunt through the Illinois country, Kentucky, and Tennessee. Back in southwest Virginia he met [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone). In 1773 he went with Boone's first attempt to settle in Kentucky, which ended when Boone's son James was killed.

His most famous ride came the next summer. In 1774 war broke out on the frontier, the conflict now called [Dunmore's War](/stories/treaty-of-camp-charlotte-1774/). Virginia surveyors were scattered across Kentucky, laying off land for veterans. The governor wanted them warned and brought home.

Capt. William Russell of the Clinch settlements chose Boone for the job, and Boone chose Stoner. The pair crossed the mountains and searched the Bluegrass and the Falls of the Ohio. They found that most surveyors had already fled, and they overtook one party on the way home by Cumberland Gap. Boone later wrote that they made "a tour of eight hundred miles, through many difficulties, in sixty-two days," according to a [Winchester Sun history column](https://winchestersun.com/2020/07/31/where-in-the-world-who-was-michael-stoner/).

In 1775 Stoner helped Boone blaze the trail to [Boonesborough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boonesborough,_Kentucky) for [Richard Henderson](/people/#richard-henderson)'s Transylvania Company. He lived at the fort for several years as one of its meat hunters, and he was badly wounded in an attack there in 1777.

People remembered him as a short, chunky man of great endurance. His brother-in-law said Stoner was only a fair shot at a target, "but at game, he was the best man in Kentucky."

In 1776 Stoner claimed 1,400 acres southeast of present [Paris](/stories/paris-from-hopewell/), and built a cabin and raised corn there. The stream became Stoner Creek. He later sold the claim and settled in the Bush Settlement of Clark County, where Stoner Branch still carries his name. He married Frances Tandy Tribble, daughter of Rev. Andrew Tribble.

In old age he hunted and trapped in Missouri, partly alongside Boone. He died in Wayne County. The Winchester Sun gives 1813, and other accounts give 1814 or 1815.

## Kentucky today

Fort Boonesborough State Park in Madison County has a reconstructed fort near the site where Stoner hunted and was wounded. In Bourbon and Clark counties, Stoner Creek and Stoner Branch still carry his name.
